cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Experimental questions reward careful reasoning more than memorised apparatus
names.
We will analyse original classroom observations, not pretend we performed
these
experiments.
Use an illustrative vernier with least count zero point zero two millimetres.
Its main scale reading is twelve millimetres and the seventh vernier division
coincides.
The raw reading is twelve point one four millimetres.
When correctly closed, this instrument reads positive zero point zero four
millimetres.
What correction should we apply?
Pause and think about a ruler that adds an unwanted amount.
Subtract that positive zero error.
Corrected diameter is twelve point one zero millimetres.
If a diameter is used in a cylinder volume calculation, its error matters
twice
to first order because diameter is squared.
Volume is pi d squared L divided by four.
For small worst case bounds, fractional volume uncertainty is approximately
twice diameter uncertainty divided by diameter, plus length uncertainty
divided
by length.
Let corrected diameter be twelve point one zero plus or minus zero point zero
two millimetres and length forty point zero plus or minus zero point one
millimetres.
Assume those are the stated bounds after correction, including any relevant
zero correction uncertainty.
The resulting fractional bound is about zero point zero zero five eight one,
or
zero point five eight one percent.
This linear bound is not a root sum square statistical uncertainty.
Do not switch rules without knowing what the question specifies.
Repeated measurements can reveal random scatter, but taking many readings does
not remove a wrong zero setting.
Record units, raw values, corrections
and the stated uncertainty model separately.
Real instrument work should be supervised and follow the laboratory procedure;
this lesson develops observation and calculation skills without asking you to
operate unfamiliar equipment.
For a simple pendulum at small angular amplitude, period is two pi times the
square root of length divided by g.
Square it and you get a straight line relation: T squared equals four pi
squared divided by g, times length.
Plot T squared vertically against length horizontally.
A slope of four seconds squared per metre gives g equal to four pi squared
divided by four, approximately nine point eight seven metres per second
squared.
Illustrative points at lengths zero point four, zero point six, zero point
eight and one metre have T squared values one point six, two point four, three
point two and four seconds squared.
Their slope agrees.
Those are constructed teaching data, not a claim of real measured precision.
Why time several oscillations?
A timing uncertainty of zero point two seconds on one period is much more
significant than on twenty periods.
For a one metre pendulum with approximate period two seconds, twenty
oscillations take forty seconds.
Divide total time by twenty.
If the stated total time bound is zero point two seconds, the period bound is
zero point zero one seconds.
Suppose length uncertainty is zero point zero zero two metres.
Since g is proportional to L divided by T squared, its small worst case
fractional uncertainty is length uncertainty over length plus twice period
uncertainty over period.
That is zero point zero zero two plus zero point zero one, or one point two
percent.
A graph fit can use several lengths, but a wrong pivot to centre length or
timing bias still matters.
Check small amplitude, timing convention and the graph intercept.
The JEE skill is connecting what you observe to the slope and its units, not
just inserting a period into a formula.
Now a measurement trap: the instrument is part of the circuit.
Connect a voltmeter across a one kilo ohm resistor.
Let the voltmeter's resistance be ten kilo ohms, and put the ammeter outside
that parallel pair so it reads both currents.
If the measured voltage is one volt, resistor current is one milliampere and
voltmeter current is zero point one milliampere.
The ammeter reads one point one milliamperes.
Dividing voltage by that reading gives about nine hundred nine point one ohms,
smaller than the actual one thousand.
You measured the parallel combination, not the resistor alone.
A different placement can introduce the ammeter's series resistance instead.
Always draw the instrument connections before choosing a correction.
Next, consider an ideal uniform metre bridge of total wire length one hundred
centimetres.
Unknown resistance X is in the left gap, known resistance two ohms in the
right.
Balance length measured from the left is forty centimetres.
The null condition gives X over two equals forty over sixty.
Hence X is four thirds ohms.
At null, the galvanometer current is zero because its terminals have equal
potential; the supply and bridge wire currents generally are not zero.
If the only small uncertainty were plus or minus zero point one centimetres in
that balance length, with known resistance and total wire length treated as
exact, the fractional X bound would be one hundred times zero point one
divided
by forty times sixty.
That is about zero point four one seven percent.
End corrections, wire nonuniformity, contacts and known resistor tolerance
require extra treatment in a real setup.
Keep these assumptions visible.
Never connect a classroom bridge or diode experiment directly to household
mains.
Practical work belongs in a supervised, appropriately rated low voltage
laboratory.
